item.title: Engineering signal transduction for closed-loop gene and cell therapies.
item.abstract: Chronic diseases are still treated largely with interventions that are constitutive, intermittently administered and poorly aligned with real-time physiology. Synthetic biology is changing this paradigm by treating gene circuits as programmable genetic software that can be deployed across cellular therapeutic hardware spanning from prokaryotic to eukaryotic systems, including probiotic cells, designer cells, immune cells and stem‑cell‑derived platforms. In this framework, engineered systems can sense disease-associated signals, compute them through synthetic or repurposed transduction pathways and adjust therapeutic output to maintain physiological variables within a desired range. Closed-loop therapeutics therefore begin to merge diagnosis, treatment and prevention within the same living platform. Across metabolism, inflammation, infection, cardiovascular regulation and cancer, early mammalian systems show that endogenous sensing, intracellular computation and therapeutic actuation can be combined in clinically relevant architectures. The emerging concept of setpoint medicine captures the clinical ambition of these systems: not simply to deliver a dose, but to keep physiology within an interpretable and therapeutically desirable range. Realizing this vision will require durable and modular control circuits, hardware-aware delivery strategies, interpretable safety frameworks, controller-style performance metrics and increasingly AI-assisted design, calibration and oversight. If these challenges can be met, the future of therapy may be defined less by intermittent dosing than by the continuous control of physiology.

item.title: A CD7-targeted AAV variant enables efficient T and NK cell engineering in vivo.
item.abstract: Adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors have been applied for precise genome engineering in human T cells but poor tropism restricts their efficiency and translational potential. Here, through directed evolution of the AAV6 capsid in primary human T cells, we identified a family of variants containing an APR motif at residues 455-457. The lead candidate, AAV.APR31, enabled robust transduction of primary T and NK cells at nearly 100-1,000-fold lower doses than AAV6 and outperformed the human T cell-tropic capsid AAV-hT7. CRISPR screening identified CD7 as a lineage-specific entry enhancer alongside the canonical AAVR pathway and structural analysis suggested that the APR motif facilitates CD7 engagement. Unlike existing delivery systems confined to one engineering mode, AAV.APR31 enabled transient transgene delivery, site-specific knock-in and transposon integration in human T and NK cells, generating CAR-T cells functionally equivalent to lentiviral vector-manufactured products. Systemic administration of AAV.APR31-generated CAR-T cells in vivo resulted in potent tumor control in hematologic and solid tumor mouse models.

item.title: An engineered probiotic with integrated biocomputation and multi-molecular recording for precision theranostics of colitis.
item.abstract: Engineered therapeutic microbes capable of sensing and responding to diseases offer transformative potential for precision medicine. However, their capacity to intelligently process the complex and dynamic biomarkers of multifaceted diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) remains limited. Here, we design a probiotic system that executes logic computations through four stage-specific inflammatory biomarkers, enabling precise diagnosis and closed-loop treatment of colitis in mice. Integration with a CRISPR-based molecular recorder allows dynamic tracking of biomarker levels and converts inflammatory signals into quantifiable, site-specific base-editing events, thereby achieving precise diagnosis and analysis of disease progression within a living mammalian gut. We additionally develop a multimodal machine-learning classifier that utilizes both bioluminescent reporter signals and sequencing data to accurately stage intestinal inflammation with an accuracy of 0.83 ± 0.05. Together, this work provides a robust platform for in situ biocomputation and marks a significant advance toward intelligent, precision theranostics for gastrointestinal disorders.

item.title: Characterization of the SsdA deaminase-family for improved cytosine base editors.
item.abstract: The choice of a suitable cytosine deaminase is a key decision when designing a base editor. Recently, bacterial toxins with cytosine deaminase activity have been established to build potent base editors for genome editing. Among those, SsdA gained considerable traction, being highly active and among the smallest established deaminases for cytosine base editors. The toxic nature of SsdA presents the major challenge, making wild type SsdA unsuitable for base editing. Although several modifications of SsdA are available, a comparison and deeper understanding of these modifications is still missing. Here, we investigate and compare the effects of several SsdA modifications. We enable a more educated choice for researchers by characterizing several improved SsdA variants for base editing. Amino acid substitutions at a key residue in SsdA suggest that steric alterations relieve its toxic effects. Indeed, the in vitro deaminase activity of SsdA was negatively linked to its in vivo performance. This indicates that base editing performance is highly compromised by toxic side effects, making less active deaminase variants the better genome editing tools. We further characterized a set of SsdA homologous proteins and showed that they were similarly toxic as SsdA. Two of them were confirmed to be cytosine deaminases and one of these allowed the construction of a new, highly functional base editing tool. This work deepens our understanding on DYW-family cytosine deaminases and broadens their use for genome editing.

item.title: Securing Cell-Free Expression: Safeguards for Distributed Biomanufacturing.
item.abstract: Cell-free expression (CFE) is an acellular biomanufacturing platform capable of producing diverse biomolecules, including proteins, enzymes, and mRNA, outside of living cells. Unlike traditional bioproduction, which requires sterile culture systems and large-scale bioreactors, CFE enables rapid, modular, and decentralized synthesis. CFE extracts can be freeze-dried, stored for extended periods, and reactivated on demand by simply adding a nucleic acid template. This makes it particularly suited for point-of-need applications such as diagnostics, vaccines, and potentially therapeutics in remote, resource-limited, or emergency settings. However, the same features introduce novel biosecurity concerns. Commercially available CFE kits already support the production of bacteriophages and virus-like particles with minimal specialized equipment. As benchtop DNA synthesis and CFE technologies become increasingly accessible, barriers of skill, facilities, and resources are significantly reduced, enabling malicious actors or small autonomous groups to generate harmful biological agents. To address these risks while enabling safe deployment, we recommend: (1) investing in yield optimization and the development of modular, good manufacturing practice-compatible CFE units for distributed manufacturing (performance and scalability); (2) engineering CFE systems with bioorthogonal or otherwise nontransferable components to reduce potential misuse (intrinsic safety feature); and (3) implementing risk-based restrictions for different CFE formulations, balancing innovation with security oversight (tiered access controls). By combining these measures, CFE can be responsibly integrated into global health security infrastructure, delivering its transformative benefits without compromising biosecurity.

item.title: Genetically encoded chemically controlled proximity switches: Molecular design, pharmacology, and therapeutic considerations.
item.abstract: Genetically encoded chemically controlled proximity systems are chemogenetic tools that utilize small molecules to regulate protein association, higher-order assembly, and dissociation. Over the past three decades, an expanding repertoire of these systems has transformed the study of protein function and cellular signaling by enabling rapid, reversible, and tunable manipulation of protein localization, assembly, activity, and downstream physiological processes. As these technologies advance from experimental tools toward therapeutic applications, their translational potential depends not only on molecular switch performance but also on the properties of the chemical inducer and engineered protein components. In this review, we summarize the major classes and design principles of representative genetically encoded chemically controlled proximity systems, with particular emphasis on the pharmacological determinants that define their therapeutic operating window, including pharmacodynamic orthogonality, pharmacokinetics, tissue exposure, endogenous target engagement, and clinical readiness. We also examine how the biological origin and engineering of the chemogenetic modules influence immunogenicity and long-term compatibility. We further discuss exemplary applications, including pharmacological control of CAR-T cell activity, programmed cell death, CRISPR-based genome and epigenome engineering, and on-demand secretion of therapeutic proteins. Finally, we consider the delivery and coordinated expression of chemically regulated protein components as major remaining barriers to therapeutic implementation and highlight clinically compatible inducers, compact and minimally immunogenic protein modules, de novo protein design, and advances in viral and nonviral delivery as promising directions toward more reliable and pharmacologically tractable chemically controlled therapies.

item.title: Synthetic biology-enabled development of bioactive natural product therapeutic leads.
item.abstract: Synthetic biology opens new avenues for developing and discovering natural products of therapeutic value in a sustainable manner. Traditional 'grind and find' bioactivity-guided fractionation approaches tend to pose challenges including rediscovery of known compounds, low production yields, and lack of ability to generate analogs for drug development. This perspective covers key examples of using synthetic biology strategies to overcome such barriers through generating difficult-to-source compounds, exploring the chemical space, harnessing next-generation hosts for improved synthesis, and modularizing the biosynthetic pathway for efficient manipulation and optimization. We highlight key examples of synthetic biology applied to develop therapeutically relevant natural products from the main classes of natural products: terpenes, polyketides, nonribosomal peptides, and ribosomally synthesized and posttranslationally synthesized peptides. Taken together, these new approaches provide access to complex and difficult-to-source natural products to develop next-generation medicines.

item.title: KiNG, a reversibly photoactivatable green variant of the fluorescent protein mNeonGreen.
item.abstract: Photoactivatable fluorescent proteins are indispensable tools in fluorescence imaging, yet the green-emitting subset remains the least developed and, until now, has contained no derivative of mNeonGreen, one of the brightest monomeric green fluorescent proteins reported to date. Twelve rounds of directed evolution of mNeonGreen yielded KiNG (kindling mNeonGreen), a reversibly photoactivatable green variant. In solution, blue light (395-470 nm) converts KiNG into a bright fluorescent form with a photoactivation contrast of 41, which relaxes thermally to the dark form with a half-time of 14 min at 310 K; activation at 470 nm is 7.5 times faster than at 395 nm. Parental KiNG cannot be switched off by light of any wavelength tested, a behaviour attributable to its anomalously low chromophore pKa of 4.3 and the consequent absence of a protonated chromophore form. The protein retains 73% of the molecular brightness of EGFP in vitro and photoactivates efficiently in mammalian cells, where it permits sequential two-colour activation together with the red photoactivatable protein PAmCherry1 and the measurement of cytoplasmic diffusion coefficients in HEK293T cells. Crystal structures of KiNG in the non-photoactivated and photoactivated states at 2.30 and 2.19 Å resolution, together with site-directed mutagenesis, establish that photoactivation proceeds by light-driven trans-to-cis chromophore isomerization accompanied by concerted rearrangement of five residues lining the chromophore cavity, followed by thermal cis-to-trans relaxation. Two features are unprecedented among reversibly switchable fluorescent proteins: rotation of Pro67, which exchanges its stacking partner between the chromophore tyrosine ring and His68/Trp169, and Cα-C rotation of the Phe73 main-chain carbonyl, which accommodates repositioning of the imidazolinone ring and forms a new hydrogen bond to the displaced Glu47.

item.title: Engineering antimicrobial peptides through the design-build-test-learn framework.
item.abstract: The rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance has intensified the need for alternative anti-infective strategies. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) offer diverse mechanisms of action, but their translation remains constrained by poor physiological stability, host toxicity, and manufacturing costs. This review examines AMP development within a design-build-test-learn (DBTL) framework that connects computational discovery, peptide production, experimental evaluation, and iterative optimization. Proteome mining and generative artificial intelligence expand the accessible sequence space, while solid-phase synthesis, engineered microbial hosts, and cell-free systems convert selected sequences into testable molecules. Chemical modification and formulation provide complementary routes to improve stability and delivery. Standardized screening and in vivo studies then establish the evidence needed to prioritize candidates and inform subsequent design and production decisions. Throughout this cycle, activity must be optimized together with toxicity, stability, manufacturability, and delivery rather than treated as the sole measure of success. This review discusses applications in medicine, agriculture, food preservation, and biotechnology, and identifies remaining limitations in data quality, assay comparability, scale-up, and translational support. The DBTL framework provides a basis for coordinating these activities, although its practical value depends on experimentally validated feedback and application-specific development criteria.

item.title: Synthetic biology approaches to overcoming the rhizobium competition problem in legume agriculture.
item.abstract: Rhizobia are soil-dwelling bacteria that infect legume plants, inducing the formation of organs called nodules. Within nodules, rhizobia convert atmospheric nitrogen gas to ammonia, providing the plant with an accessible nitrogen source. Rhizobial inoculation has long been recognized as a tactic for providing nitrogen to legume crops; however, the effectiveness of inoculants is often limited by competition from other soil microbes. To overcome this "rhizobium competition problem", the usage of inoculant strains that are both high-quality symbiotic partners and more competitive than native strains has been suggested. Here, we suggest avenues through which synthetic biology (SynBio) could be used to engineer increased competitiveness into elite inoculants. Considering a few select mechanisms (Nod factor biosynthesis, bacteriocin production, stress tolerance, motility, and metabolism), we review the current literature with promising evidence for SynBio interventions, and we emphasize that the effects of genetic manipulations should be evaluated under the lens of the broader soil community. We also describe recent developments in the rhizobial SynBio toolkit, which will facilitate more precise genome edits across diverse rhizobia. In summary, a growing body of research is exposing the intricacies of rhizobial competitiveness, leaving opportunities for SynBio strategies to enhance competitiveness and develop more efficacious inoculants.

item.title: Loss of riboflavin biosynthesis leads to accumulation of select aromatic amino acids and loss of infectivity in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
item.abstract: Riboflavin biosynthesis is required for in vitro survival of the human pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb). However, despite the lack of a known transporter, growth can be rescued by exogenous riboflavin. The riboflavin biosynthesis pathway is also predicted essential in vivo, but whether riboflavin levels available in the host can support survival has not been directly tested. Here we constructed a set of inducible CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) knockdown and targeted gene deletion strains for known riboflavin biosynthesis genes (ribA2, ribG, ribH, ribC) as tools to characterize riboflavin requirements, uptake, and metabolite changes and to assess in vivo essentiality. We found that riboflavin, but not flavin adenine dinucleotide or flavin mononucleotide, rescued auxotrophy for all strains tested. Further, riboflavin uptake was not affected by disruption of proton motive force or ATP synthesis, suggesting that uptake is not via an active mechanism. Targeted metabolite profiling after removal of riboflavin from growth medium confirmed reduced riboflavin levels. While other riboflavin intermediates were not detected, significant accumulation of aromatic amino acids (Phe, Tyr) was observed across all assayed strains, as well as alteration in a vitamin B9 metabolite. Selecting the ribC knockout as a representative strain, we found that riboflavin depletion had a bacteriostatic effect as late as 3 weeks after removal. Unexpectedly, {Delta}ribC lacked infectivity in an aerosol mouse infection, suggesting that the potential to scavenge riboflavin from the host is not sufficient to survive in vivo. Overall, our results show that altered metabolism upon loss of riboflavin biosynthesis leads to compromised Mtb infectivity.

item.title: Construction of an engineered Salvia miltiorrhiza hairy root line for heterologous biosynthesis of ginsenosides F1 and Rg1 via multi-gene co-expression.
item.abstract: Ginsenosides, major bioactive constituents of Panax notoginseng, possess diverse pharmacological activities, but their supply from field cultivation is constrained by long growth cycles and low yields. Compound Danshen preparation, composed of Salvia miltiorrhiza, P. notoginseng, and borneol, requires sustainable production of its active components. Here, an engineered S. miltiorrhiza hairy root line, designated "S. miltiorrhiza Hairy Root 1.0 (SHR 1.0)", was generated by integrating the heterologous notoginsenoside pathway into S. miltiorrhiza hairy roots, which natively produce tanshinones and phenolic acids. Using Golden Gate assembly, a PPT vector harboring SmSE, SmDDS, PnPPDS, and PnPPTS was constructed to establish protopanaxadiol (PPD) and protopanaxatriol (PPT) production in PPThr lines, with maximum contents of 36.36 μg/g DW for PPD and 28.60 μg/g DW for PPT in different lines. Introduction of an Rg1 vector carrying four glycosyltransferase genes (Pn1-31, Pn3-29, Pn3-31, and Pn3-32) enabled ginsenosides F1 and Rg1 production, with the Rg1-3 line accumulating the highest levels of both F1 (8.90 μg/g DW) and Rg1 (17.54 μg/g DW). Transcriptomic analysis revealed extensive transcriptional changes, EV itself showed substantial transcriptional changes relative to WT, indicating a transformation-associated background; Rg1-3 showed additional pathway-associated changes. Untargeted metabolomic profiles differed among WT, EV, and Rg1-3. Relative to EV, most features were not significantly changed, whereas relative to WT about half differed, consistent with a transformation background. No KEGG pathway based on the differential metabolites remained significant after pathway-level multiple-testing correction. In the untargeted dataset, L-phenylalanine showed decreased abundance and tanshinone I showed increased abundance in Rg1-3 relative to both WT and EV. The tanshinone I increase was also confirmed by targeted HPLC. Collectively, these data indicate a limited set of pathway-associated metabolite changes rather than a broad metabolic disturbance. This study represents a proof-of-concept for the production of selected representative components in a heterologous plant hairy root chassis and provides a basis for further exploration of hairy root-based plant systems as a complementary approach to microbial platforms.

item.title: Friedelin in plants: metabolism, synthase engineering and production strategies.
item.abstract: Friedelin (FD) is a pentacyclic triterpenoid with significant pharmacological potential and serves as the biosynthetic precursor to the anti-obesity drug celastrol. Despite its value, FD availability is limited by low natural abundance and the stereochemical complexity of chemical synthesis. This article critically reviews the state-of-the-art in FD research, spanning natural distribution, extraction methodologies, and the molecular basis of its biosynthesis. The structural evolution of friedelin synthases (FDSs), contrasting the mechanisms of multifunctional versus single-function enzymes, was analyzed. Furthermore, a comprehensive roadmap for sustainable production, integrating "Push-Block-Regulate-Store" metabolic engineering strategies with novel insights into transcriptional regulation, was provided. It is proposed that the convergence of AI-driven enzyme design, transporter engineering, and CRISPR-based precision breeding will overcome current yield bottlenecks, enabling the industrial-scale biomanufacturing of FD and its derivatives.

item.title: Tandem duplication of oxidosqualene cyclases and enzyme promiscuity of cytochromes P450 contribute to the diversity of triterpenoids in Eleutherococcus senticosus.
item.abstract: Triterpenoid saponins in Araliaceae plants exhibit remarkable structural diversity, with species-specific compounds like ginsenosides and ciwujianosides, yet the genetic basis remains elusive. Here, we report a chromosome-scale genome assembly of Eleutherococcus senticosus (Rupr. & Maxim.) Maxim. (1.39 Gb, 51,243 genes) and demonstrate that it shares a lineage-specific whole-genome duplication (WGD-α, Ks = 0.112) with Hedera helix. Phylogenomic analyses reveal a 4:4 syntenic relationship between these species, confirming their close evolutionary relationship. Notably, both E. senticosus and H. helix lack the dammarenediol-II synthase (DDS) gene, explaining the absence of ginsenoside-type saponins. Through genome mining and functional validation, we identify eight OSC genes, including a tandemly duplicated cluster on chromosome 18 unique to E. senticosus. Biochemical assays show that EsOSC4 and EsOSC12 synthesize tirucalla-7,24-dien-3β-ol, representing the first enzymatic characterization of a tirucallane synthase in Araliaceae, while EsOSC13 produces lupeol. Site-directed mutagenesis establishes residue 372 (valine in EsOSC13, methionine in EsOSC4/12) as critical for this functional divergence. Moreover, we discover three promiscuous CYP716 enzymes (EsCYP716A244/A450/A452) capable of oxidizing β-amyrin, lupeol, and tirucalla-7,24-dien-3β-ol at multiple positions, generating diverse oxidized derivatives. These findings reveal tandem duplication and enzyme promiscuity as primary mechanisms driving triterpenoid diversity in E. senticosus, with implications for synthetic biology applications in saponin production.

item.title: Detoxification Functions of Cytochrome P450 Genes in Insects: A Systematic Review.
item.abstract: Cytochrome P450 (CYP450) is a ubiquitous class of catalytic enzymes that mediate the metabolism of xenobiotics and the synthesis/degradation of endogenous compounds in insects, supporting essential physiological processes. Recent advancements in high-throughput sequencing and molecular biology have significantly expanded our understanding of CYP450 functions across diverse animal taxa. This review synthesizes current research progress on the detoxification roles of insect CYP450s against pesticides, plant secondary metabolites, and heavy metals, providing critical references for gene discovery and functional characterization. Furthermore, it establishes a foundational framework for investigating detoxification mechanisms of toxic substances in insects. Future studies should focus on elucidating the functional diversity and regulatory networks of P450s through integrative approaches combining multi-omics, structural biology, and synthetic biology. These efforts will drive the development of precision-targeted green pest management strategies, offering novel solutions for sustainable agricultural practices.
